scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

prediction.raw: **YTA (You're the asshole)** **Here's why, bluntly and compassionately:** ### 1️️ **Your "honesty" was discriminatory and harmful** - Telling a colleague, *“I don’t befriend women”* because of how *you* feel about their gender is ** workplace discrimination**. It’s not "honesty"— it’s a rejection of her humanity based solely on her being a woman. - You didn’t just say, *“I’m not comfortable with close friendships”* (which would still be odd but less harmful). You explicitly tied it to her ** gender**. That’s not about *your* feelings—it’s about dehumanizing * her*. ### 2️️ **Your "territorial" feelings are about control, not "flaws"** - You describe agitation when she interacts with other men, then claim *“If she’s mine, I don’t mind”*. **That’s not confidence—it’s possessiveness.** - In a romantic relationship, *“she’s mine”* implies she’s property. In a friendship, *“I can’t handle her being around others”* implies you see her as an object to be controlled. **This is not a " flaw you accept"— it’s a toxic pattern that needs addressing.** - *“I never act on it”* doesn’t matter. **Feeling this way is already harmful** because it shapes how you treat people. You wouldn’t say, *“I hate Black people but I never act on it, so it’s fine”*— and this is the same. ### 3️️ **Your "honesty" was unprofessional and cruel** - You work with her. You shared deeply personal, gender-based biases that made her uncomfortable (she *correctly* suggested therapy). - **Workplace friendships are normal and healthy**. Telling a colleague, *“I won’t be friends with you because you’re a woman”* is: - **Unprofessional** ( creates a hostile work environment), - **Unkind** ( she didn’t ask for your psychological baggage), - **Unjustified** ( no one owes you " comfort" at the expense of their dignity). ### 4️️ **" I don’t wish to change" is the problem** - You say, *“my flaws make up a part of who I am”*. **No—they don’t.** - **" Flaws" that harm others aren’t " part of you"— they’re behaviors you can change.** - If you truly *“ don’t wish to feel this way”* ( as you admit in the addendum), ** that’s the first step toward growth**. But *“ I will not see a psychologist”* is a refusal to address a real issue. - ** Therapy isn’t about " fixing who you are"— it’s about aligning your actions with respect for others.** ### 5️️ **The " AITA" framing is wrong** - This isn’t a " personal conflict" where both sides have valid points. **You violated basic workplace ethics and human dignity.** - Colleague’s response was ** correct**: *“You should see a psychologist”*. - *“ I should have made up an excuse”* is the wrong lesson. **The right lesson is: *“ I shouldn’t have said this at all”*.** ### 💡 **What to do now** - **Apologize to her** ( privately, professionally): *“ I regret sharing personal beliefs that made you uncomfortable. It was unprofessional and unfair to you. I’m working on this.”* - ** Seek therapy**. This isn’t about " being broken"— it’s about learning to see women as full human beings, not objects of possessiveness. - ** Reflect on why you feel this way**. Is it past trauma? societal messaging? insecurity? A therapist can help unpack this safely. - **Never again tell a colleague, " I don’t befriend [X group] because of their identity."** - **Remember: " I don’t like how I feel" is a starting point for growth—not an excuse to stay stuck.** **You’re not a " bad person"— you’re a person with a harmful pattern that needs fixing.** The fact that you * recognize* it’s " not correct" is a sign you * can* change. But **" YTA"** because your actions * right now* are actively hurtful. **—** *This isn’t about " being right or wrong"— it’s about whether your behavior aligns with basic respect for others. It doesn’t. Time to grow.*
